A hash table is a way of organizing stored information so that a lookup can often go almost directly to the right place, rather than searching through everything. Imagine a long shelf divided into numbered compartments. Each stored item has a key—a name or identifier—and a value—the information associated with it. The table needs a rule that turns each key into a compartment number. That rule is the hash function. It is not supposed to be secret or especially meaningful; it is a deterministic recipe that takes the key and produces an integer. The integer is then reduced, usually with a modulo operation, to an index within the array of compartments. Those compartments are the buckets. A bucket can hold one entry or, when two keys map to the same index, several entries.

The important point is that the hash function does not store the key in a special sorted position determined by the key's meaning. It merely gives a repeatable starting point. For lookup, the table takes the key being sought, applies exactly the same hash function, reduces the result to the same bucket index, and goes to that bucket. If the bucket is empty, the key cannot be present—assuming the table is consistent—and the lookup can stop immediately. If the bucket contains one key-value pair, the table compares the sought key with the stored key. If they match, it returns the associated value. The comparison matters because the hash value is only a clue; it is not proof of identity. Different keys can produce the same bucket number, which is called a collision.

Collisions are normal. Since a finite array has fewer buckets than potential keys, and even a very good hash function can map two keys to the same bucket, the table needs a collision strategy. Chaining is one common strategy. Each bucket is not limited to a single entry; it can hold a small collection of entries, traditionally a linked list, though implementations may use arrays or other structures. A lookup that lands on such a bucket checks each entry in the collection in turn, comparing the stored key with the sought key and stopping when it finds a match. If it reaches the end without a match, the key is absent. This comparison is essential: if two different keys land in the same bucket, the hash alone cannot tell which one is wanted.

A small made-up example can show the process. Suppose a table has five buckets, numbered zero through four, and suppose we use a deliberately invented hash assignment—not a real hash function, just an illustration—under which cedar goes to bucket 2, maple goes to bucket 4, and pine also goes to bucket 2. Then bucket 4 contains maple alone, while bucket 2 contains cedar and pine in a chain. To look up maple, the table applies the made-up assignment, gets bucket 4, sees maple there, compares the key maple with the stored key maple, and returns maple's value. To look up pine, the table gets bucket 2, finds a chain containing cedar and pine, compares cedar first and finds it does not match, then compares pine and finds the match, returning pine's value. If the sought key were, say, oak and the invented rule also sent oak to bucket 2, the table would examine cedar, then pine, find neither match, and conclude that oak is not present. If oak were sent to an empty bucket, the lookup would conclude absence even faster.

The efficiency of all this depends on how many entries end up in each bucket. The load factor is the number of stored entries divided by the number of buckets. A load factor of 0.5 means that, on average, each bucket holds half an entry; a load factor near 1 means buckets are, on average, nearly full. As entries are added, the load factor rises, chains tend to lengthen, and lookups may need more comparisons. To keep lookups fast, a hash table typically resizes when the load factor crosses a chosen threshold, often something like 0.75. Resizing means allocating a larger array of buckets and reinserting the existing entries according to the same hash rule, now reduced modulo the new bucket count. Existing entries must be rehashed because changing the number of buckets changes which bucket each key maps to. This work is relatively expensive for the insertion that triggers it, but it is occasional, and afterwards the load factor is lower again.

Under good conditions, lookup is expected to be constant time. If the hash function spreads keys roughly evenly and the load factor is kept bounded, a typical bucket contains only a small number of entries—often zero or one, with occasional short chains. The lookup computes the hash in constant time, jumps to a bucket in constant time, and compares a small, bounded number of entries. The average or expected work does not grow proportionally with the total number of stored entries, so we call it expected constant time, or average-case constant time.

That does not mean every lookup is guaranteed to be constant time. In the worst case, a poor hash function, an unlucky set of keys, or deliberate adversarial input could send many or all keys to the same bucket. Then that bucket's chain contains a number of entries proportional to the total number stored. Finding a key in such a chain may require comparing every entry, so the lookup becomes linear in the number of entries. This is the worst-case linear behavior. Chaining still works correctly in that case; it simply loses the speed advantage that made the hash table attractive. Good hash functions, sensible resizing, and attention to adversarial inputs are what make the expected constant-time behavior the normal outcome rather than a mere hope.

That is how the lookup finds its way.
